definition: A measure of how quickly a chemical reaction takes place — how fast reactants are used up or products are formed.
The theory that states reactions occur when reactant particles collide with sufficient energy (at least the activation energy) and the correct orientation.
The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur. Reactions with high activation energies are slower.
A collision between reactant particles that results in a chemical reaction. Particles must have enough energy and the correct orientation.
The amount of substance dissolved per unit volume of solution. Increasing concentration increases the rate of reaction by increasing the number of particles per unit volume.
A measure of the average kinetic energy of particles. Increasing temperature increases the rate of reaction because particles move faster and collide more frequently and with more energy.
The total area of a solid exposed to a reactant. Increasing surface area (e.g. by using smaller pieces) increases the rate of reaction because more particles are exposed for collisions.
A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up. It works by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
For reactions involving gases, increasing pressure increases the concentration of gas particles, increasing collision frequency and the rate of reaction.
A substance that decreases the rate of a chemical reaction by interfering with the catalyst or reducing the chance of successful collisions.
A reaction in which the products can react together to reform the original reactants. Shown by the symbol ⇌ in the equation.
The state reached in a closed system when the forward reaction and reverse reaction occur at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
Describes whether the equilibrium favours the products (right) or the reactants (left). Affected by changes in temperature, pressure, and concentration.
If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the equilibrium will shift to oppose that change and restore equilibrium.
A system in which no substances can enter or leave. Required for dynamic equilibrium to be established.
Rate of reaction can be measured by recording the change in mass, volume of gas produced, or colour change over time.
An insoluble solid formed in a solution. The disappearance of a cross viewed through a precipitate forming can be used to measure reaction rate.
Calculated as: quantity of reactant used (or product formed) ÷ time taken. Gives an average rate over the course of the reaction.
